title: Joshua 6:1–14
context: Joshua 6:1–14 opens with Jericho shut tight against Israel. The LORD declares that he has already given the city into Joshua’s hand and lays out an unusual plan: the armed men, seven priests with rams’ horn trumpets, and the ark are to march around the city once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh, ending with a long blast and a great shout. The ark, the symbol of the LORD’s presence, is at the center of the procession. The march is silent until Joshua gives the word. Both traditions read the account as a lesson that victory comes from the LORD and is received through obedience.

verses.text: Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the children of Israel. No one went out, and no one came in.
verses.arminianNotes: Jericho is tightly shut up, with no one going out and no one coming in. Arminian readers note that the city’s response to the news of the Jordan is to bar its gates against Israel, in contrast with Rahab, who responded to the same news with faith in Israel’s God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the human impossibility of the situation: a fortified city closed against an army with no siege equipment. Both traditions read the verse as setting up a victory that can only be credited to the LORD, not to Israel’s strength or strategy.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and the mighty men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Joshua that he has given Jericho into his hand, speaking of the victory as already accomplished. Arminians see God’s promise calling for Israel’s trusting obedience: the gift is certain, but Israel must still march as commanded to receive it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress the certainty of God’s word, which speaks of a future victory as already done. Both traditions hold God’s sovereign gift and Israel’s required obedience together here, and neither treats Israel’s obedience as making the promise uncertain.

verses.text: All of your men of war shall march around the city, going around the city once. You shall do this six days.
verses.arminianNotes: All the men of war are to march around the city once each day for six days. Arminian readers note that the command tests patience and trust, since nothing visible happens for six days and the people must keep obeying without seeing results.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the repetition as an ordained means through which God chooses to give the victory. Both traditions read the strange plan as making clear that the outcome rests on God’s word, not on military calculation, and that his people obey even when the method seems foolish.

verses.text: Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the ark. On the seventh day, you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets.
verses.arminianNotes: Seven priests bear seven rams’ horn trumpets before the ark, and on the seventh day they march seven times. Arminians note the repeated number seven, often associated with completeness, and the priests’ central role, which marks the whole event as worship rather than ordinary warfare.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that rams’ horns were associated with Israel’s sacred occasions, such as the jubilee announcement (Leviticus 25:9). Both traditions read the pattern of sevens and the ark at the center as framing the conquest of Jericho as the LORD’s holy act.

verses.text: It shall be that when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, and when you hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people shall shout with a great shout; then the city wall will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, every man straight in front of him.”
verses.arminianNotes: At the long blast, the people are to shout, the wall will fall down flat, and every man will go straight in. Arminians stress that God announces the outcome beforehand, so that Israel’s shout becomes an act of faith in what he has promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the shout as the response God ordained, not the cause of the wall’s fall. Both traditions read the verse in light of Hebrews 11:30, which attributes the fall of Jericho’s walls to faith, and both see faith resting on God’s prior word.

verses.text: Joshua the son of Nun called the priests, and said to them, “Take up the ark of the covenant, and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the LORD’s ark.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua the son of Nun calls the priests and tells them to take up the ark of the covenant with seven priests bearing trumpets before it. Arminians note Joshua’s faithful passing on of exactly what the LORD said, without adding or changing anything.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress the ark as the visible sign of the LORD’s presence going before his people, as at the Jordan (Joshua 3:11). Both traditions see God’s covenant presence, not Israel’s army, at the center of the march.

verses.text: They said to the people, “Advance! March around the city, and let the armed men pass on before the LORD’s ark.”
verses.arminianNotes: The command goes out to the people to advance and march around the city, with the armed men passing on before the LORD’s ark. Arminian readers see the whole community joining in obedience, each group taking its assigned place in the procession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the ordered arrangement around the ark, recalling the camp arrangement in Numbers 2. Both traditions see God’s people organized around his presence, with soldiers, priests, and people sharing one act of obedience.

verses.text: It was so, that when Joshua had spoken to the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams’ horns before the LORD advanced and blew the trumpets, and the ark of the LORD’s covenant followed them.
verses.arminianNotes: As Joshua speaks, the seven priests advance before the LORD and blow the trumpets, with the ark of the LORD’s covenant following. Arminians note that the priests blow "before the LORD," a phrase that treats the ark’s presence as the LORD’s own presence among them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and observe the immediate obedience that follows Joshua’s word. Both traditions read the verse as a picture of worship in action, with the covenant God leading his people and the trumpets proclaiming his presence.

verses.text: The armed men went before the priests who blew the trumpets, and the ark went after them. The trumpets sounded as they went.
verses.arminianNotes: The armed men go before the priests, the ark follows, and the trumpets keep sounding. Arminian readers see a careful order: the soldiers guard the procession, but the focus remains on the ark and the priests, showing whose battle this is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The verse repeats the details of the procession in a slow, liturgical style. Both traditions see the repetition emphasizing that every part of the march follows God’s design, and that Israel’s strength is not the point of the account.

verses.text: Joshua commanded the people, saying, “You shall not shout nor let your voice be heard, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua commands the people not to shout or speak until the day he gives the word. Arminians see disciplined restraint as part of faith: the people wait silently on God’s timing instead of boasting or complaining, unlike the murmuring of the wilderness generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that silence leaves only the trumpets, the sign of the LORD’s presence, to be heard. Both traditions read the command as teaching that God’s people wait on his word and speak when he gives the signal, not before.

verses.text: So he caused the LORD’s ark to go around the city, circling it once. Then they came into the camp, and stayed in the camp.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s ark goes around the city once, and the people return to the camp for the night. Arminian readers note the anticlimax of the first day, which tests whether the people will keep trusting a plan that produces no visible result.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the ark’s circuit as central, since the text says Joshua caused the LORD’s ark to go around the city. Both traditions see God’s presence encircling Jericho as the real action of the day, even though nothing seems to change.

verses.text: Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the LORD’s ark.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua rises early, and the priests take up the LORD’s ark again. Arminians see diligence in Joshua’s early rising, a pattern elsewhere in the book (Joshua 3:1; 7:16; 8:10), showing a leader eager to obey God’s instructions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the verse as part of the steady rhythm of obedience over the six days. Both traditions see faithful leadership modeled in Joshua’s consistency as he repeats what God commanded day after day without visible results.

verses.text: The seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams’ horns in front of the LORD’s ark went on continually, and blew the trumpets. The armed men went in front of them. The rear guard came after the LORD’s ark. The trumpets sounded as they went.
verses.arminianNotes: The seven priests keep blowing the trumpets in front of the ark, with armed men ahead and the rear guard behind. Arminian readers see the community’s perseverance: the people keep the same order and keep obeying, which the narrative treats as faith in action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the rear guard completes the picture of the ark protected on every side. Both traditions read the detailed repetition as underlining that Israel did exactly as the LORD commanded, without improvising.

verses.text: The second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. They did this six days.
verses.arminianNotes: On the second day they march around once and return, and they do the same for six days. Arminians stress the patience required by repeated, outwardly fruitless obedience, a lesson for believers who must keep trusting God without immediate results.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the six days of marching lead to a seventh day of completion. Both traditions see faithful perseverance as the fitting response to God’s promise, and the narrative compresses the days to move toward the climax.
